sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the basics of cybersecurity and why protecting electronic health information matters.
- Recognize phishing, social engineering, and other common cyber threats.
- Protect credentials, protected health information, and devices using appropriate safeguards.
- Report suspicious activity, security incidents, and potential breaches promptly according to policy.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Cybersecurity is like having locks and alarms on a house so only the right people can get in and nothing valuable is stolen or broken.

### Question 2

Think of the CIA triad as three promises: keep secrets secret (confidentiality), keep information correct (integrity), and keep it available when needed (availability).

### Question 3

A medical record is like a treasure chest that holds a person's name, address, and insurance numbers — thieves want it because it has everything they need to pretend to be that person.

### Question 4

The Security Rule is a set of rules for keeping electronic health information safe, like a rulebook for locking digital filing cabinets.

### Question 5

Administrative safeguards are the 'people rules' — who is trained, what the policies say, and who is responsible — rather than locks or software.

### Question 6

Physical safeguards are the locks, doors, and cabinets that stop someone from walking up and grabbing records or a computer.

### Question 7

Technical safeguards are the 'computer rules' — logins, automatic sign-outs, and secret codes that scramble data.

### Question 8

A unique user ID is like signing your name on every chart you open, so everyone knows who did what.

### Question 9

Leaving a computer logged in is like leaving your house key in the door — the right move is to pull it out right away.

### Question 10

A strong password is like a key that only fits one lock and that you never lend to anyone.

### Question 11

MFA is like needing both a key and a secret knock to open a door — having just one is not enough.

### Question 12

Your login is like your personal signature — you would not let someone else sign your name on a chart.

### Question 13

Hiding a password under the keyboard is like hiding a house key under the doormat — everyone knows to look there.

### Question 14

Shoulder surfing is like someone reading your diary over your shoulder while you write in it.

### Question 15

Locking your computer when you step away is like locking your car even when you only run inside for a minute.

### Question 16

A clean desk rule is like putting toys away in a locked box so no one can take them while you are gone.

### Question 17

Encryption is like writing a message in a secret code that only the person with the decoder ring can read.

### Question 18

Sending PHI insecurely is like mailing a private letter on a postcard where anyone can read it — encryption puts it in a sealed envelope.

### Question 19

Phishing is like someone dressing up as your teacher to trick you into telling them a secret.

### Question 20

General phishing is like a fishing net cast wide, while spear phishing is like aiming a single arrow at one specific fish.

### Question 21

Whaling is named for hunting whales — the biggest, most valuable targets in an organization, like the boss.

### Question 22

Vishing is a 'voice' scam — someone calling and pretending to be your bank or a coworker to get secrets.

### Question 23

Smishing is like getting a fake note that looks like it is from your bank asking for your secret PIN.

### Question 24

Pretexting is like making up a believable story — 'I'm from IT and I need your password' — to get someone to hand over a secret.

### Question 25

Baiting is like leaving a free cookie that is secretly full of something bad, hoping someone cannot resist picking it up.

### Question 26

Tailgating is like slipping in behind someone through a door before it closes, without showing your own key.

### Question 27

A real friend writes your name on a card; a stranger sending the same card to everyone just says 'Dear Customer.'

### Question 28

Scammers say 'hurry, hurry!' because they do not want you to stop and think — like a pushy stranger rushing you into a decision.

### Question 29

A scammer can buy a website name that is one letter off from the real one, like getting 'payrol' instead of 'payroll,' to fool you.

### Question 30

Hovering over a link is like checking the address on an envelope before opening the letter inside.

### Question 31

An .exe file is a little program that can do bad things when opened — like accepting a wrapped package from a stranger without checking inside.

### Question 32

If someone emails asking to change where money goes, call the number you already trust to double-check — like confirming with a friend before lending money to a stranger.

### Question 33

A fake login page is like a fake ATM that looks real but records your card number instead of giving you money.

### Question 34

This is like someone pretending to be the boss and asking you to hand over the office's secret files to a stranger.

### Question 35

If you see a suspicious email, the safe move is to show a grown-up (your IT team) instead of poking it yourself.

### Question 36

When you spot something fishy, you tell the right helper — the IT team — not just anyone.

### Question 37

If you touch something hot, you tell someone right away so they can help — hiding it only makes it worse.

### Question 38

A phishing drill is like a fire drill — practicing in a safe way so everyone knows what to do in a real emergency.

### Question 39

Ransomware is like a thief who locks your diary in a box and says they will only give back the key if you pay them.

### Question 40

Ransomware scrambles your files into secret code and hides the key, like locking everything in a safe and keeping the combination.

### Question 41

Ransomware usually sneaks in when someone opens a poisoned email attachment or link — like a trap behind a tempting door.

### Question 42

Paying a kidnapper does not guarantee they will return what they took — and it tells them the crime works, so they do it again.

### Question 43

A backup is like keeping a spare copy of your homework at home, so if someone scribbles on your school copy, you still have a clean one.

### Question 44

An offline backup is like keeping a spare key in a completely different, hidden place — the thief cannot grab both.

### Question 45

Antivirus is like a guard dog that barks when something bad tries to get into your computer.

### Question 46

Updating software is like fixing a broken lock on your door before a burglar notices it.

### Question 47

A firewall is like a security guard at the door who checks who is allowed in and out of the building.

### Question 48

Least privilege is like giving each worker only the keys to the rooms they actually need to enter, not every key in the building.

### Question 49

When someone leaves a job, taking back their keys and keycard keeps the building safe — the same goes for computer logins.

### Question 50

An audit log is like a guest book at a museum that writes down exactly who went into which room and when.

### Question 51

Using open public Wi-Fi with private information is like shouting a secret in a crowded room where anyone can listen.

### Question 52

A VPN is like a secret underground tunnel that carries your messages safely past the people who might be watching the road.

### Question 53

A strange USB drive is like a mystery package left on your porch — you should not plug it in without knowing where it came from.

### Question 54

Shredding is like tearing a secret letter into tiny pieces so no one can put it back together and read it.

### Question 55

De-identification is like removing the name tag from a picture so you can share it without revealing who it is.

### Question 56

Minimum necessary means only telling the part of a secret that the other person actually needs to know — nothing extra.

### Question 57

If a pipe bursts, you call for help right away — hiding it only lets the water spread.

### Question 58

Stopping a leak first, then calling the experts, is the right order — you stop the water before mopping.

### Question 59

A shared login is like everyone signing their papers with the same name — no one can tell who really did what.

### Question 60

Each person uses their own keycard to clock in and out, so the office knows who was where and when.

### Question 61

Working with patient information at home is like doing secret work — you need a private, locked space, not the kitchen table.

### Question 62

Protecting a phone with PHI is like keeping a wallet with a lock, a secret code, and a way to erase it if it is lost.

### Question 63

A patient portal is like a personal mailbox with a key, so each patient can see only their own letters.

### Question 64

Faxing safely is like double-checking the address before mailing a secret letter, so it goes to the right person.

### Question 65

Sending PHI securely is like putting a letter in a locked, sealed envelope rather than a postcard anyone can read.

### Question 66

You would not hand a friend's secret to someone who just claims to know them — first you check they are really allowed to know.

### Question 67

Before sharing a secret, you check the person is really who they say they are and is allowed to know.

### Question 68

If a stranger calls and demands a secret 'right now,' the safe move is to check with a trusted source first, not to hurry and hand it over.

### Question 69

You would not hold a locked door open for a stranger at home — the same rule protects the clinic's private areas.

### Question 70

Keep your screen turned like a diary you do not want the person next to you to read.

### Question 71

You turn a screen away like you would turn a private letter away from someone standing beside you.

### Question 72

Throw away a secret by shredding it, not by tossing it where anyone can find it.

### Question 73

If you lose something with a secret inside, you tell someone right away so they can help lock it down.

### Question 74

If a computer gets locked by a bad guy, you do not pay — you call for help and do not touch the trap.

### Question 75

A scary pop-up telling you to call a strange number is like a stranger knocking and saying 'pay me to fix your house' — you check with the real experts instead.

### Question 76

If you think someone knows your locker combination, you change it right away and tell the teacher.

### Question 77

A strong password is like a long, secret sentence that no one could guess, instead of something simple like '1234.'

### Question 78

Using the same password everywhere is like using one key for your house, car, and locker — if someone copies it once, they can open everything.

### Question 79

MFA is like needing both a key and a special code from your phone to open a door — stealing the key alone is not enough.

### Question 80

The Privacy Rule says who may see health information; the Security Rule says how to lock up the electronic version.

### Question 81

HIPAA says everyone who handles patient information has to learn the rules for keeping it safe — like a class before you drive.

### Question 82

Breaking the rules has consequences — the office must respond with fair discipline so everyone knows the rules matter.

### Question 83

If a text about a package looks suspicious, check the real website yourself instead of tapping the link — like asking the store directly instead of trusting a stranger's note.

### Question 84

Defense in depth is like a castle with a moat, walls, guards, and locks — if one fails, the others still protect it.
